justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modestly bullish baseline view on the asset, with prices drifting slightly higher across the three horizons from roughly 113.8 at one day out to 115.0 at one month. The near-term estimate was anchored primarily by recent price momentum and prevailing market conditions at the time of the forecast, assuming no major catalysts would materialize within 24 hours. The one-week estimate incorporates a small upward drift consistent with a mild positive trend, while the one-month estimate extends that drift further, reflecting an assumption that underlying fundamentals or broader market conditions support gradual appreciation. The incremental increases are intentionally modest because I did not want to overstate directional conviction, especially at longer horizons where mean reversion and noise dominate.

The confidence interval widths expand substantially as the horizon lengthens, which reflects the well-established statistical reality that uncertainty compounds over time. At one day, the 90% interval spans roughly 5.2 units, reflecting relatively tight short-term price dynamics where intraday volatility is bounded. By one week, that interval nearly doubles to about 11.4 units, capturing the possibility of meaningful macro news, earnings releases, or sentiment shifts. At one month, the interval widens to 22 units, acknowledging that over four weeks, a wide range of economic data, policy decisions, and market regime changes could materially alter the trajectory. Historical volatility of the asset class was the primary input governing these width choices.

Several specific risks could push outcomes outside these stated intervals in either direction. On the upside, a surprise positive catalyst — such as better-than-expected economic data, a dovish policy pivot, or a sector-specific positive development — could drive prices well above the upper bound of my one-month interval of 126. On the downside, a macro shock such as a sudden escalation in geopolitical tensions, a credit event, or an unexpected hawkish policy move could easily breach the lower bound of 104. Liquidity conditions also matter; in thin markets, price dislocations can be sharp and fast, rendering even wide confidence intervals insufficient.

It is worth acknowledging that my intervals are probabilistic statements, not guarantees. A stated 90% confidence interval means I expected roughly a 10% chance of outcomes falling outside the range, so tail events breaking through the bounds are entirely consistent with the forecast being well-calibrated. If the asset exhibits fat-tailed return distributions — which many financial instruments do — the true probability of extreme outcomes may be somewhat higher than a Gaussian-based model would suggest. I would encourage treating the outer bounds of these intervals as soft guardrails rather than hard limits.
